items.title: 68087_Cliff Leeman oral history interview
items.q: My association with Charlie Barnet was 1940. The last of '39 and '40 -- and he gave me all the freedom in the world, all the freedom.

ctx.x: What were you saying about Charlie Barnet?

My association with Charlie Barnet was 1940. The last of '39 and '40 -- and he gave me all the freedom in the world, all the freedom. The band had been burned out in California; Duke Ellington had given them all the rope that they needed -- that was the style of band that they wanted, and all my life I knew this, I could have played with Duke Ellington without any parts because I knew every part by heart, and I wanted Charlie Barnet who just said play -- and he gave me all the freedom to develop my own style at…

items.title: 52150_Charlie Barnet oral history interview
items.q: Cliff Leeman was there for a while

ctx.x: Who else was in that band?

Well, let's see. Tiny -- well, Cliff Leeman was there for a while, but then Tiny Kahn took over on the drums, a beautiful man, left us very prematurely. And Eddie Safranski was playing bass, and Carlos Vidal had the bongos and the conga, mostly conga. And Claude Williamson was the piano player. And we had, let's see, Obie Masingill, Dick Kenney -- the other couple of trombone players escape

me. Let's see, there was Lenny something playing the alto saxophone player. Dick Hayfer, tenor. Dave Matthews, tenor. No, Dick Hayfer took Dave Matthews place. Kurt Bloom was playing the other tenor, and Reuben Leon, who's now a union official in L.A. Everybody gets old, don't they? Well, that's about it. The trombones -- I can't remember the other two.
